q: Rinapatra, the loan-deed forms recording debtor, creditor, amount and rate of interest, are found in which body of ancient literature?
explain: Rinapatra (rinalekhya) loan deeds appear in the Vedic literature (Vedas, 2000-1400 BCE), the earliest Indian texts to mention usury.

q: What does the term usury mean?
options: Lending money at an excessive rate of interest
explain: Usury is the practice of charging an excessive rate of interest on loans; the Vedas are the earliest Indian texts to mention it.

q: The adesha, an order to a banker to pay a sum to a third person, resembles a modern bill of exchange. It belongs to which era?
explain: The adesha was an instrument of the Mauryan period (321-185 BCE). The Mughal-era credit instrument was the hundi (and the dastawez loan deed).

q: The concept of the modern banking system was first conceptualised by the people of Italy under which name?
explain: The word bank traces to the Italian Banco, under which the modern banking system was conceptualised. Hundi, adesha and baratte are Indian instruments.

q: Which two important innovations did ancient Greece and the Roman Empire add to banking?
options: Insuring deposits and fixing interest rates
explain: Greece and Rome added acceptance of deposits and money changing. The earlier Mesopotamian banking involved grain loans.

q: Which of the following is NOT counted among the indigenous bankers of India?
explain: Indigenous bankers include shroffs, seths, mahajans and chettis. Presidency Banks were modern banks set up under East India Company charters.

q: Which of the following is NOT a defect of indigenous banking?
options: They charge very high rates of interest
They follow modern methods of financial accounting
They do not distinguish between short-term and long-term finance
explain: Indigenous bankers used local accounting practices that could not match modern financial accounting, so following modern methods is not one of their defects.

q: Loan deeds of the Mughal era were called:
explain: Rinapatra was Vedic and adesha Mauryan. In the Mughal era loan deeds were dastawez; hundi is a credit instrument that evolved alongside.

q: Dastawez-e-miadi was a loan deed payable:
options: Only on the death of the debtor
explain: Dastawez-e-miadi was payable after a fixed time, whereas dastawez-e-indultalab was payable on demand.

q: Payment orders issued by royal treasuries in the medieval period were known as:
explain: Barattes were payment orders used by royal treasuries; dastawez were loan deeds.

q: The Bank of Hindustan, regarded as the first bank of modern banking in India, was set up in which year?
explain: The Bank of Hindustan was founded in Calcutta in 1770 by M/s Alexander and Co and ceased to operate in 1832. 1806 is the year of the first Presidency Bank.

q: The Bank of Hindustan, Calcutta, ceased to operate in:
explain: It was founded in 1770 and wound up in 1832.

q: The first Presidency Bank was originally established under which name?
explain: The Bank of Calcutta (1806) was renamed Bank of Bengal on 2 January 1809.

q: How much of the total capital of the Bank of Bengal (₹50 lakh) was the share of the East India Company?
explain: The Bank of Bengal had a total capital of ₹50 lakh, of which ₹10 lakh was subscribed by the East India Company.

q: Which Presidency Bank was formed by amalgamating several existing regional banks and headquartered in Madras?
explain: The Bank of Madras (1 July 1843), the third Presidency Bank, came from the amalgamation of several regional banks.

q: Which Presidency Bank was started on 15 April 1840?
explain: Bengal came in 1806, Bombay on 15 April 1840 and Madras on 1 July 1843.

q: The Imperial Bank of India was formed on 27 January:
explain: The Imperial Bank of India (1921) was created by amalgamating the three Presidency Banks and later became SBI in 1955.

q: Which of the following banks was NOT amalgamated to form the Imperial Bank of India?
explain: Imperial Bank combined the three Presidency Banks. The Bank of Hindustan had ceased in 1832.

q: Which bank became the State Bank of India in 1955?
explain: The Imperial Bank of India was nationalised in 1955 and renamed State Bank of India.

q: When was the State Bank of India established?
explain: SBI came into being on 1 July 1955 under the SBI Act 1955. 1 April 1935 is the date RBI began working.

q: Among the banks that exist today, which is the oldest bank of India?
explain: SBI traces its origins to the Bank of Calcutta (1806) through the Imperial Bank, so it is the oldest existing bank.

q: In which year was the concept of limited liability introduced in India, leading to joint stock banks?
explain: Limited liability came in 1860; joint stock banks followed, though many were undercapitalised.

q: The Bank of Upper India, the oldest joint stock bank of India, was established in:
explain: The Bank of Upper India was set up in 1863 and failed in 1913. Allahabad Bank followed in 1865.

q: Which is considered one of the oldest joint stock banks that still works and also one of the oldest public sector banks?
explain: Allahabad Bank, founded by British on 24 April 1865, was merged with Indian Bank in 2020. The other three banks failed.

q: Which bank, set up in Lahore in 1894, was the first bank purely managed by Indians?
explain: PNB was founded in Lahore in 1894 by Lala Lajpat Rai and others. Central Bank (1911) was the first wholly Indian-owned commercial bank.

q: Who among these was one of the founders of Punjab National Bank in Lahore?
explain: Lala Lajpat Rai, Babu Purshotam Lal Tandon and S. Dayal Singh were among PNB's founders. Mehta and Pochkhanawala are linked with the Central Bank of India.

q: In India, the first limited-liability bank managed by an Indian board, founded in 1881, was:
explain: The Oudh Commercial Bank, set up at Faizabad in 1881, was the first limited-liability bank with an Indian board; it failed in 1958.

q: Which bank is known as the first truly Swadeshi bank of India?
explain: Central Bank of India (1911), founded by Sir Sorabji Pochkhanawala, was the first commercial bank wholly owned and managed by Indians.

q: Who was the first Chairman of the Central Bank of India?
explain: Sir Sorabji Pochkhanawala founded Central Bank of India and Sir Pherozeshah Mehta was its first Chairman.

q: Which was the first Indian bank to open a branch abroad (London, 1946)?
explain: Bank of India, founded as a private entity in 1906, opened the first foreign branch in London in 1946.

q: Which public sector bank completed 100 years of its establishment on 21 December 2011?
explain: Central Bank of India was founded in 1911, so it completed a century in December 2011.

q: In which year did the Hilton-Young Commission submit its report recommending a central bank?
explain: The Hilton-Young Commission reported in 1926; the RBI Act followed in 1934 and RBI began on 1 April 1935.

q: Which objective was set out in the recommendations of the Hilton-Young Commission for a central bank?
options: To separate the control of currency and credit from the government
To fix the price of gold
To start the Five Year Plans
explain: The Commission wanted currency and credit control separated from the government, and banking facilities widened across the country.

q: The Reserve Bank of India began functioning on:
explain: RBI was created by the RBI Act of 1934 and began operations on 1 April 1935 as banker to the central government.

q: Which committee, set up by RBI after Independence, recommended taking over the Imperial Bank of India?
options: All India Rural Credit Survey Committee
explain: The All India Rural Credit Survey Committee proposed taking over the Imperial Bank and integrating former state-associated banks with it, leading to SBI.

q: How many commercial banks were there in India in 1950-51?
explain: The book gives 430 commercial banks in 1950-51. The figure 600 refers to the larger number of banks in the pre-Independence modern era.

q: The SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act that let SBI take over five former state-associate banks was passed in:
explain: The State Bank of India Act was passed in 1955, and the Subsidiary Banks Act in 1959.

q: Which of the following was NOT one of the five subsidiary banks listed as taken over by SBI under the 1959 Act?
explain: The five were Patiala, Hyderabad, Travancore, Bikaner and Jaipur, and Mysore. Bharatiya Mahila Bank was a much later bank that merged with SBI in 2017.

q: In the subsidiary-bank arrangement of 1959, what share of capital was held by SBI?
explain: SBI owned 55 per cent and the old shareholders kept 45 per cent.

q: The Deposit Insurance Corporation of India (Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, 1961) was established in:
explain: The DIC was set up in January 1962 to protect the deposits of small depositors.

q: The National Credit Council (NCC), set up in February 1968, was meant to:
options: Help the Government and RBI reallocate credit according to plan priorities
explain: NCC assisted the Government and RBI in reallocating credit in line with plan priorities.

q: Cooperative banks were brought within the regulations of the RBI in:
explain: Cooperative banks came under RBI regulation in 1966, the year in which the rupee was devalued for the first time.

q: The Lead Bank Scheme aims to provide adequate banking and credit in rural areas through which approach?
options: A service area approach, with one bank assigned to one area
A uniform interest-rate approach for all banks
A deposit-insurance approach for each village
explain: The Lead Bank Scheme (introduced 1969) assigns one bank to one area under a service area approach.

q: How many banks were nationalised in 1969, each with deposits of over ₹50 crore?
explain: Fourteen banks were nationalised in 1969. Six more (liabilities above ₹200 crore) followed on 15 April 1980.

q: Six banks were nationalised on 15 April 1980. What criterion applied?
options: Demand and time liabilities above ₹200 crore
explain: The 1980 criterion was demand and time liabilities greater than ₹200 crore (as on 14.03.1980); in 1969 it was deposits above ₹50 crore.

q: The Differential Rate of Interest (DRI) scheme was introduced in 1972 for:
explain: DRI offered loans at concessional interest to cater to the weaker sections and their upliftment.

q: The Priority Sector concept was set up for private sector banks in:
explain: The concept applied to public sector banks in November 1974 and to private sector banks in November 1978.

q: The Board for Financial Supervision (BFS) was set up within RBI in 1994 to:
explain: The BFS was created inside RBI exclusively for supervision of banks and related entities.

q: The Banking Ombudsman is a quasi-judicial authority created to resolve complaints of:
explain: The Ombudsman was created to enable resolution of complaints by bank customers.

q: Which body, set up in 2006, takes voluntary registration of banks that commit to customer service as per agreed standards?
options: Banking Codes and Standards Board of India (BCSBI)
explain: BCSBI was set up in 2006 for voluntary registration of banks committed to agreed customer service standards.

q: The IFSC is an 11-character code. The fifth character is the digit zero, reserved for:
explain: The first four letters are the bank name, the fifth is 0 reserved for future use, and the last six identify the branch.

q: The merger of 10 public sector banks into 4 came into effect from:
explain: The plan announced in August 2019 took effect on 1 April 2020.

q: Which bank merged into Canara Bank in the 2020 consolidation?
explain: Syndicate Bank merged into Canara Bank. Allahabad merged with Indian Bank; Corporation with Union Bank; Dena with Bank of Baroda.

q: Indian Bank was merged with which bank in the 2020 consolidation?
explain: Allahabad Bank merged into Indian Bank. Andhra went to Union Bank and United Bank to PNB.

q: Union Bank of India absorbed which pair of banks in 2020?
options: Oriental Bank of Commerce and United Bank
explain: Union Bank merged with Andhra Bank and Corporation Bank. OBC and United went to PNB.

q: Oriental Bank of Commerce and United Bank of India were merged into which bank?
explain: With OBC and United Bank merged in, PNB became the second largest public sector bank after SBI.

q: Dena Bank and Vijaya Bank were merged with which bank, creating the third-largest bank by loans?
explain: The Dena-Vijaya merger into Bank of Baroda was proposed on 17 September 2018 and approved on 2 January 2019.

q: The five associate banks of SBI and Bharatiya Mahila Bank merged with SBI with effect from:
explain: The SBI group merger took effect on 1 April 2017, making SBI the country's largest lender.

q: How many public sector banks remained after the 2020 merger, as per the list in the book?
explain: After the 10-into-4 consolidation, 12 PSBs remained: six anchor banks and six independent banks. In 2017 there were 27.

q: Which of the following was among the six independent public sector banks, not merged in 2020?
explain: The independents were Indian Overseas Bank, UCO Bank, Bank of Maharashtra, Punjab and Sind Bank, Bank of India and Central Bank of India.
